item.title: Reaching separated flow states by release and recapture with learned latent feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.10208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Targeting a prescribed flow configuration rather than an aerodynamic coefficient is challenging because the desired state may lie outside the natural attractor. We demonstrate cluster-based control in a learned vorticity representation for two-dimensional flow over a NACA0015 airfoil at $Re=500$ and $\alpha=15^\circ$, using a localized streamwise momentum source near the leading edge. An actuation-enriched ensemble is compressed with a variational autoencoder and partitioned into macrostates. We optimize a continuous feedback law interpolating macrostate-dependent amplitudes without an explicit latent dynamical model. For an attached target, the optimized law approaches constant forcing, arrests vortex shedding and maintains the attached state. For a strongly separated target, the law instead establishes attachment, withdraws actuation so that the natural separation transient carries the flow through the target, and restores forcing to recapture attachment. Over the evaluation horizon, the closed-loop trajectory revisits the target approximately every three shedding periods. Companion open-loop calculations isolate the arrest, release and recapture processes.
item.dc:creator: Khalid Rafiq, Aditya G. Nair

item.title: Tuning fluid frictional drag through flow-induced aggregation of wormlike micelles
item.description: arXiv:2611.10365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Charged amphiphilic surfactants are versatile polymorphic molecules which can form supramolecular structures, such as wormlike micelles. We study the rheology and non-Newtonian fluid dynamics of the cationic surfactant trimethyltetradecylammonium chloride (TTAC) combined with the aromatic counter-ion sodium salicylate (NaSal). In the non-dilute regime, this solution exhibits a linear viscoelastic response consistent with a single-mode Jeffreys model, and in capillary pinch-off experiments, fluid filaments form extended cylindrical threads, indicating strong strain-stiffening. In the dilute regime the linear viscoelasticity and extensional rheology become immeasurably small, but the TTAC/NaSal mixture develops flow-induced structures at high shear rates, as the result of an end-to-end concatenation of micelles produced by shear-induced flow alignment. These flow-induced structures augment both the measured viscosity and the viscous drag in laminar flows at high shear rates (by as much as 50 %). In turbulent Taylor-Couette flow, the flow-induced structures produce a sudden and dramatic destabilizing influence on the stable toroidal Taylor vortices, resulting in upwards of a 200 % enhancement in turbulent drag. However, with increasing Reynolds number, the turbulent flow transitions smoothly to a state of drag reduction, generating up to a 30 % reduction in fluid frictional drag but without the shear-induced degradation that plagues drag reduction strategies based on solutions of high molecular weight polymer, such as polyacrylamide. These results show that surfactants are a unique and effective modifier of fluid frictional drag in both laminar and turbulent flow regimes, capable of producing both significant levels of drag enhancement and drag reduction by tuning the composition and operating conditions.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Warwaruk, Amanda Tiano, Berith Isaac, Gareth H. McKinley

item.title: Reconstructing Interacting Blood Flow and Wall Interface Deformation from Noisy Flow Data Using PirateNets
item.description: arXiv:2611.10505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blood flow and elastic vessel-wall motion interact with each other: fluid stress drives wall deformation, while the moving wall changes the domain in which blood flows. Given noisy flow images, we study the inverse problem of reconstructing the coupled, unsteady three-dimensional motions. We solve the reconstruction through Gauss--Seidel-type alternating fluid and geometry updates. For the fluid, we use physics-informed networks to recover velocity and pressure by fitting the observations while enforcing the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations on the moving domain, which is described by an arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) map. For the geometry, a reference-domain correction and sequential registration recover the vessel shape and wall displacement. Interface traction continuity and an elastic momentum equation regularize the registration so that the recovered displacement is also physics-informed. The networks evaluate fields and physical residuals at sampled space--time points without remeshing the moving domain. Experiments on a converging channel and a patient-like aorta demonstrate reconstruction of flow and wall motion from noisy data. Ablation and parameter-sensitivity studies examine the role of structure regularization and imperfect physical coefficients. A further experiment with a three-element Windkessel outlet condition demonstrates how the framework accommodates a more physiologically realistic boundary setting.
item.dc:creator: Han Zhang, Xue-Cheng Tai, Alessandro Veneziani, Raymond H. Chan

item.title: Cable construction effects on the lateral forces and wakes of helically stranded cables under oblique inflow
item.description: arXiv:2611.11286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Helically stranded cables in aerial towing systems experience oblique inflow, but are often modeled as smooth cylinders, neglecting three-dimensional cross-stream coupling and surface texture. We perform large-eddy simulations and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition for a smooth cylinder and four stranded cables at four inclinations from $22.5^\circ$ to $90^\circ$, all stationary, with $Re \approx 1.0 \times 10^4$. Aerodynamic differences are governed mainly by cross-sectional symmetry and strand-scale groove depth. Force-source decomposition shows that surface pressure contributes 94.9%--98.3% of the mean normal force and dominates the mean lateral force. High-symmetry, quasi-circular envelopes maintain balanced circumferential pressure, whereas deep-grooved, low-symmetry tri-lobed geometries produce asymmetric separation and a persistent lateral pressure imbalance. In the wake, high-symmetry cables sustain spanwise-synchronized Karman shedding at moderate-to-high inclinations, concentrating fluctuation energy in a dominant low-rank mode. Deep grooves disrupt shedding coherence, deflect the recirculation zone laterally, and spread energy across broadband scales. Mean lateral force and lateral-force fluctuations are therefore decoupled: the quasi-circular $(1 \times 19)$ cable has minimal mean lateral force but strong periodic fluctuations, while the deep-grooved $(3 \times 7)$ cable has weak fluctuations but appreciable mean lateral force. These results support construction-dependent cable selection and aerodynamic load modeling.
item.dc:creator: Tielin Ma, Junlin Zhang, Jingcheng Fu, Chongwen Jiang, Chuan Ye

item.title: Flash evaporation Riemann Problem: Thermodynamic Relaxation and Oscillation-Free Real Fluid Finite Volume Method
item.description: arXiv:2611.11315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Flash evaporation Riemann problem (FeRP) formulated the wave structures of flash evaporation in the vapor-liquid homogeneous equilibrium limit. However, physical flash evaporation involves finite-rate interphase heat and mass transfer, inducing the wave structure to deviate from the equilibrium state. To solve such a non-equilibrium Riemann problem, this paper first derives the governing equation of mechanical equilibrium evolution in a relaxation system, based on which an oscillation-free Homogeneous Relaxation Real Fluid (HRRF) finite volume method is developed. In addition to the Euler equations with mass relaxation, the HRRF method evolves advection equations for the internal energy--pressure affine parameters and the vapor volume fraction, in order to eliminate numerical pressure oscillations inherent in conservative methods while preserving phase-transition-induced pressure changes, and consistently degenerate into a completely pressure-equilibrium method in supercritical flows. The HRRF method is then employed to comprehensively evaluate how thermodynamic relaxation affects the FeRP solution. Results indicate that the non-classical expansion shock of the FeRP loses its traveling-wave characteristics with increasing relaxation time, continuously degenerating into a self-similar rarefaction wave. Compared with the equilibrium limit, an increased mass transfer relaxation time smooths the expansion branch of the RP solution, lowers the intermediate pressure and velocity, and induces a pseudo-splitting of the rarefaction wave as well as a pseudo-advance of the phase transition onset. Meanwhile, the heat transfer relaxation time primarily dictates the temperature difference in the vapor-liquid mixture, thereby modulating the liquid superheat and in turn influencing the mass transfer rate.
item.dc:creator: Haotong Bai, Ping Yi, Yixin Yang, Guoyan Zhao, Wenjia Xie, Mingbo Sun

item.title: Hydrograd v2.0: a differentiable two-dimensional shallow-water model on unstructured meshes with steady and unsteady adjoints for calibration and closure learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.11540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present \textit{Hydrograd} v2.0, a significantly improved differentiable 2D shallow-water model written in Python with JAX. The model solves the shallow-water equations on the unstructured meshes of production models such as SRH-2D and HEC-RAS 2D with a well-balanced, positivity-preserving finite-volume scheme that handles wetting and drying. Gradients are tailored to the type of problem. Steady states are found by Newton's method with an exact sparse Jacobian obtained by graph colouring, and their gradients follow from the implicit function theorem at the cost of one linear solve. Unsteady flows are differentiated in reverse mode with checkpointing, or with an implicit time integrator whose gradient costs about two forward runs. All gradients agree with finite differences, to about $10^{-8}$ for steady flows. On the Savannah River case, the steady water surface differs from that of SRH-2D by 4.7\,mm (root mean square). Steady closure learning was 96 times faster than differentiating through time marching and reached a lower loss. An inflow hydrograph was inverted from stage records with a peak error of 2\,\%. In an unsteady roughness calibration, a singular value decomposition analysis of the sensitivity matrix showed that the stage records at the gauges are 70 to 160 times more sensitive to the total resistance of the reach than to its distribution among the roughness zones, which explains why only a gauge layout with gauges in every zone recovered all five roughness values. On one GPU, a mesh of 512,000 cells takes 7.6\,s for a forward run and 51\,s for a gradient.
item.dc:creator: Xiaofeng Liu

item.title: Thermochemical Rossby waves in rapid rotation: from swallowtail geometry to nonlinear selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.11719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When heat and solute both destabilise a rapidly rotating fluid, do their buoyancies add? Codensity models assume so, giving a straight onset diagonal; spherical shells show curved and kinked thresholds. We study the Busse--Simitev rotating annulus, whose normal modes obey an exact complex cubic dispersion relation. Combining the Bilharz criterion with the neutral-curve envelope yields, in the rapid-rotation limit, an explicit swallowtail wave front, in Arnold's sense, that bends the codensity diagonal into smooth and then kinked thresholds as the diffusivity ratio decreases. Its cusp edges lie inside the unstable domain and its exposed kink ends at the swallowtail singularity; these are singularities of wave-number selection, without coalescence of temporal eigenvalues, and the swallowtail diffusivity ratio has analytical small- and large-Prandtl-number limits. At a kink, broad, fast thermal and narrow, slow compositional Rossby waves become neutral together; hidden arcs mark the birth and merger of unstable wave-number bands. The same geometry enters nonlinear selection: mean-scalar feedback factors through neutral-arc normals and scalar responses, so the mean-profile coexistence margin vanishes with the kink angle as the waves merge. Complete cubic coefficients predict robust coexistence at a reference corner and a narrow bistable interval near merger. Exact finite-rotation corners and periodic-cell simulations confirm the coexisting waves and their invasion thresholds.
item.dc:creator: Oleg N. Kirillov

item.title: Velocity gradient tensor reconstruction from tracer orientations via Jeffery dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.11878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The velocity gradient tensor is a local quantity, but methods that obtain it by spatial differencing of the velocities of spherical tracers amplify measurement noise. We propose a method that reconstructs the velocity gradient tensor from the orientations of non-spherical tracers such as flakes and rods. Based on the Jeffery-type equation, we show that, for incompressible flow, all components of the velocity gradient tensor are uniquely determined from the orientations of four tracers and their time derivatives in the neighbourhood of a reference point (orientation-based method). The method uses neither tracer positions nor spatial differencing. It therefore requires orientation measurements only near the reference point, without requiring measurements throughout a three-dimensional region, and measurement noise is amplified only through temporal differencing. Consequently, the minimum achievable error scales as $\sigma^{1/2}$ with the noise level $\sigma$, compared with $\sigma^{1/3}$ for the positional PTV-plus-differencing approach (position-based method). Numerical tests further show that the vorticity is reconstructed more accurately than by the position-based method, whereas the strain rate is reconstructed with comparable accuracy. Finally, applying the method to spherical Couette flow, we find that the reconstruction fails where the neighbouring tracers align, which renders the inversion ill-conditioned, and that this degeneracy appears as the characteristic light-and-dark pattern familiar from flow visualization.
item.dc:creator: Isshin Arai, Tomoaki Itano

item.title: Elastic frontogenesis sets the spectra of smooth elastic turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2611.11953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most turbulent flows are sustained by inertia, which transfers energy across scales and produces characteristic power-law spectra. Yet dilute polymer solutions also exhibit turbulence when inertia is negligible: in this state, known as elastic turbulence, the velocity field remains spatially smooth while both the velocity and the polymer conformation exhibit robust power-law spectra. How a smooth flow, lacking a hierarchy of eddies, generates such multiscale structure has remained unexplained. Here we show that the missing mechanism is elastic frontogenesis, whereby the flow spontaneously organizes polymer stress into thin sheets that are stretched within their plane and compressed across their thickness, causing their amplitude to grow as they become thinner. Because the fronts are sheet-like structures, this amplification-thinning law uniquely determines the polymer conformation spectrum, while the Stokes response transfers the same geometric scaling to the velocity field, reconciling broadband spectra with spatial smoothness. Being geometric rather than model-specific, elastic frontogenesis provides an organizing principle for viscoelastic flows and the viscoelastic analogue of vortex stretching in inertial turbulence.
item.dc:creator: Marco Edoardo Rosti, Andrea Mazzino

item.title: Phase-resolved turbulence dynamics in cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsatile pipe flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.12007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct numerical simulations examine the phase-dependent turbulence dynamics of pipe flow driven by cardiac-cycle-inspired waveforms. Four cases with and without a low-flow plateau span two Reynolds-number ranges. The response follows four stages of turbulent--turbulent reorganisation. Strong acceleration suppresses transverse fluctuations and vortical activity. During acceleration and early deceleration, streamwise-normal-stress production recovers ahead of pressure--strain redistribution and radial momentum transport, allowing energy to accumulate in elongated streaks. In early deceleration, near-wall high-speed streaks develop predominantly varicose disturbances associated with Q4 sweeps, whereas outer-buffer-layer low-speed streaks develop predominantly sinuous disturbances associated with Q2 ejections. The transition exhibits distinct radial sequences: Q2-based local onset occurs progressively later towards the wall, whereas Q4-based onset is nearly simultaneous across the viscous sublayer and buffer layer, with peaks occurring successively outwards. The two responses overlap between the drag minimum and recovery maximum as redistribution intensifies markedly and multiscale momentum transport recovers rapidly. Turbulence then decays and its scales readjust. Where present, the plateau prolongs this decay and weakens the turbulence inherited by the next acceleration stage. It further delays local instability and lengthens the onset-to-peak intervals of the shear contributions. An unsteady friction decomposition links these phase-dependent dynamics to the drag response, highlighting the role of delayed turbulent shear recovery in sustaining the low-drag interval.
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Wang, Yan Bao, Benlong Wang

item.title: Parametric spatio-temporal reduced-order modelling via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Gaussian Process Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.12028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SPOD-GPR, a non-intrusive, parametric, spatio-temporal reduced-order model (ROM) that combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), Spectral POD (SPOD), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). A parametric POD first projects the high-dimensional state onto a low-dimensional subspace. The reduced trajectories are then divided into windowed sections, transformed into the frequency domain, and truncated to the most energetic frequencies. SPOD is then performed independently at each retained frequency, yielding temporally coherent modes and coefficients. The parametric dependence of the POD and SPOD bases is modelled by GPR on a local chart of the Grassmann manifold after Procrustes alignment. The SPOD modal coefficients are learned both as explicit functions of the parameters and through a parameter-conditioned autoregressive model that allows for temporal extrapolation beyond the training window. Gaussian processes are sampled jointly and pathwise via Matheron conditioning, ensuring that each predictive realization carries uncertainty quantification consistent with the posterior distribution. The method is tested on four parametric examples where the parameter values and the prediction horizon lie outside the training data: the two-dimensional anisotropic Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation in a time-periodic and a travelling-wave regime, each parametrised by one of its two coefficients; flow past a cylinder parametrised by the Reynolds number; and flow past an elliptic obstacle parametrised by its semi-axes. In all cases, SPOD-GPR reduces the normalised mean absolute error compared to a POD-GPR baseline, and improves the calibration of the predictive uncertainty, especially in the fluid flow cases, where POD-GPR is severely overconfident. This opens the way to spectral, uncertainty-aware reduced-order models for many-query and real-time applications, such as digital twins.
item.dc:creator: Guglielmo Padula, Antonio Colanera, Gianluigi Rozza

item.title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality
item.description: arXiv:2611.12045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational principles for dissipative processes come in two families: minimum principles at nonequilibrium stationary states (Helmholtz, Kirchhoff, Prigogine) and maximum principles for relaxation in continuum mechanics (Ziegler, Hackl, Fischer). We contribute to the understanding of the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) by investigating its extremal properties, and uncover the connection between the two families, whose distinction was recently made precise for diffusion: the extremal character is decided by the regime, which is either relaxation at frozen state, as in a closed system (maximum dissipation), or a driven stationary state in an open system (minimum dissipation), while the underlying Rayleighian functional is convex and minimized in both cases. We further examine the Reynolds transport theorem, a useful tool for fixing the energy rates of continua, and the role of inertia, recently argued to lie beyond the reach of Rayleighian principles. With inertia the driving force must be held fixed during the variation, which is less elegant than in the inertialess case, where it is a state function. Writing the energy rate as rates times driving forces still yields the correct equations, and an extremal statement survives whenever the frozen force does not depend on the varied rate. This holds directly for unsteady Stokes flow, and for Navier-Stokes flow after a change to material coordinates, in which the particle acceleration is the second time derivative of the state and the convective term, nonvariational in the Eulerian description, does not appear. The framework is tested on the Navier-Stokes family (Stokes, unsteady Stokes, and Navier-Stokes flow, in order of increasing complexity) and on dissipative Lagrangian mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Wolfgang Flachberger, Lukas Einkemmer

item.title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
item.description: arXiv:2611.12350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.
item.dc:creator: Fehmi Najar

item.title: N-Layer quasi-geostrophic modons in a vertically sheared flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.12433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modons, or dipolar vortices, are a form of propagating vortex solution consisting of two counterrotating regions of fluid and moving together under self-advection. They are common features of the upper ocean that can remain stable over long times, thereby transporting fluid over large distances. Here, we present a semi-analytical method for finding modon solutions in a vertically-sheared background flow using the multi-layer quasi-geostrophic framework. This method works for arbitrarily many fluid layers and builds on our previous studies of multi-layer modon solutions. We present three example of modons in a background flow, highlighting the effect of varying relative potential velocity between layers and the impact of depth-dependent potential vorticity gradients arising from surface deformation and velocity shear.
item.dc:creator: Matthew N. Crowe

item.title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.12511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical simulation of hypersonic vehicles is an attractive approach to investigate the complex phenomena involved in such technologies. For this, second-order finite volume methods (FVM) are the established method in computational fluid dynamics, with the cost of high dissipation in affordable meshes, thus needing refined ones or adaptive mesh refinements techniques to obtain accurate results. An alternative is to make use of high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods, in particular discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM), once it achieves higher formal order of accuracy on element-local polynomial bases. Therefore the goal of this work is to present the numerical simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet configuration to test and verify the applicability of the DGSEM approach for a complex hypersonic flow where shock-shock interactions occur. Results revealed to be in agreement with reference FVM solvers, thus verifying the code implementation.
item.dc:creator: Beatriz Fag\'a, Georgii Oblapenko, Yiyang Zhu, Daniel Doehring, Manuel Torrilhon

item.title: Dynamics of singular-jet formation during the collapse of drop-impact craters
item.description: arXiv:2611.12533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The collapse of a drop-impact crater that bypasses the pinch-off singularity produces exceptionally thin, high-velocity jets, often referred to as singular-jets. We perform 2D axisymmetric DNS using Basilisk, employing adaptive mesh refinement to capture the intricate flow features. The numerical results for a drop diameter of $3.64$ mm at ambient pressure match the experiments well under different impact conditions. During the crater collapse, qualitatively different dimple shapes form, including an entrapped bubble beneath the dimple. Quantitatively, an entrapped bubble with a diameter of ~210 \mu m and a jet velocity of 61.7 m/s for the singular-jet case during cylindrical dimple collapse is obtained from simulations. Subtle morphological changes in crater evolution distinguish the jetting regime, with a critical angle of 109.2 between the crater side wall and its base in the singular-jet case. The simulation provides insight into the internal flow fields, enabling us to delineate the observed phenomenon. The pressure and velocity fields reveal that the high jetting velocity is associated with the formation and rapid collapse of a nearly cylindrical dimple. The resulting pressure distribution drives a strongly upward flow near the dimple base, while the nearly parallel dimple side walls redirect radial liquid motion towards the axis. We extend the simulations into the post-entrainment region and identify another singular-jet near the upper boundary of the entrainment region. The jet reaches a velocity of 63.93 m/s and exhibits morphological characteristics similar to the first singular-jet case. A regime map is constructed from simulations spanning Weber numbers ranging from 100 to 200 and Froude numbers from 45 to 92; the updated lower and upper boundaries for the entrainment region, based on singular-jet formation, are We = 45.5\, Fr^{0.237} and We = 53.5\, Fr^{0.251}, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Nivesh Mishra, Anikesh Pal

item.title: Interception Focusing of Colloid Transport in Granular Porous Media
item.description: arXiv:2611.09947v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Colloid transport and retention in environmental granular porous media underlie groundwater resource protection from, and remediation using, biological and non-biological nano- and micro-particles (colloids). During transport, colloids periodically intercept grain surfaces and translate along them at separation distances across several tens of nm corresponding to the secondary minimum between the opposing forces of longer-range of van der Waals (VDW) attraction and shorter-range electric double layer (EDL) repulsion. Relatively weak diffusive translation of colloids supports their continued translation in secondary minimum association until they are expelled to bulk fluid at rear flow stagnation zones on grain leeward sides. We herein show that this dynamic focuses colloids into a network of fluid streamlines (incomplete mixing lamellae) that enhances their subsequent likelihood of interception with downgradient grains, i.e., increases the so-called collector efficiency (typically denoted by Greek letter eta). Interception focusing of colloids in granular porous media explains well-observed outcomes of colloid transport under environmental conditions, including nonmonotonic nonexponential profiles of retained colloids and the non-Markovian nature of extended tailing of low colloid concentrations following initial elution. Interception focusing is a fundamental process that distinguishes colloids from solutes and renders inapplicable to colloids the assumption that is often invoked for solutes of complete pore scale mixing in granular porous media.
item.dc:creator: William P. Johnson (University of Utah, Geology and Geophysics, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA), Noah G. Willis (University of Utah, Geology and Geophysics, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA), Luis A. Ullauri (University of Utah, Geology and Geophysics, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA), Bashar M. Al-Zghoul (University of California Davis, Civil and Environ. Eng., Davis, California, USA), Diogo Bolster (University of Notre Dame, Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, Notre Dame, Indiana, United States)

item.title: Conductance scaling in nanopore arrays: disentangling roles of pore arrangement and reservoir geometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.09991v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The scaling of electrical conductance with the number of nanopores, $N$, in an array is of fundamental importance for applications in membrane separation and ion transport across biological membranes, and has been the subject of longstanding disagreement in the field. Combining finite element calculations with theory, we resolve this disagreement for pores with negligible surface charge by showing that two previously conflicting predictions are each correct in their own limiting reservoir geometry: cuboidal reservoirs commensurate with the interpore spacing, for which the conductance scales linearly with $N$, and infinite reservoirs, for which the scaling is sublinear in $N$ for closely spaced pores. We show the transition between these limits with increasing reservoir size and, for infinite reservoirs, we show that a simple analytical model from electrical contact theory is mathematically equivalent to an existing point-charge capacitance model for nanopore arrays and validate its applicability against finite element and method-of-moments calculations. Using this model, we derive a characteristic coupling length, $\ell_\mathrm{c,95}$, the interpore spacing at which the array conductance reaches $95\%$ of that of the same number of independent pores. $\ell_\mathrm{c,95}$ scales linearly with pore diameter $d$, and grows with $N$ as $\sim\log N$ for linear arrays and $\sim\sqrt{N}$ for square arrays, so that pore coupling persists to surprisingly large separations in large arrays. Our work provides a general framework for predicting nanopore array conductance as a function of pore arrangement and reservoir geometry, of importance to nanofluidics research and the targeted design of functional devices.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Bair, Zachery Gottshall, Matthias Kuehne

item.title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling
item.description: arXiv:2611.10666v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embedded microfluidic cooling is a promising technology for dissipating the intense heat generated by high-performance electronic chips. However, the design and optimization of such coolers impose prohibitive computational costs when using conventional numerical solvers. Here, we present a parameterized physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a deep learning framework for rapidly and accurately predicting the thermohydraulic performance of embedded manifold microchannels. By incorporating four geometric dimensions along with three spatial coordinates as the network inputs, the proposed model enables multiphysics prediction across a continuous design space. Remarkably, our predicted velocity and temperature fields differ from finite-element simulations by relative errors of only 8.1% and 5.6%, respectively, while reducing the computational time and cost by over four orders of magnitude. Key to this framework is a composite strategy combining geometric ansatz embedding, the SOAP optimizer, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum learning scheme, which helps overcome the convergence challenges inherent in training PINNs for complex three-dimensional flows. Notably, by leveraging a highly optimized JAX backend, the network achieves convergence on a single consumer-grade GPU in less than four hours. Our approach offers a physics-consistent, real-time surrogate model that can substantially accelerate innovations in advanced microfluidic cooling of future electronics.
item.dc:creator: Weiheng Li, Zhiyao Jiang, Bai Song

item.title: A new approach to measuring both the steady flow curve and the planar extensional viscosity of complex fluids using exponential shear
item.description: arXiv:2611.10780v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We revisit the protocol known as Exponential Shear (ES), first proposed by Doshi and Dealy in 1986. This is a transient strong flow that can be readily imposed in the laboratory using commercial strain-controlled (separate motor and transducer) rheometers which accurately measure both the (exponentially) time-varying torque and normal force exerted by the sample. Numerous studies over the years have proposed competing definitions of an appropriate material function for reporting data obtained from the exponentially time-varying imposed deformation. We revisit this unresolved challenge and carefully reconsider the exponential material kinematics involved and the proper definition of the corresponding material functions. We show that by understanding the time-varying eigenvalues and eigenvectors of both the shearing kinematics and the evolving state of stress in the sample it is, in fact, possible to use an exponential shear test to quantitatively map out \textit{both} the full flow curve (of shear viscosity vs. shear rate) and the steady planar extensional viscosity curve as a function of deformation rate. These findings are supported by numerical simulations of a number of nonlinear viscoelastic constitutive models, asymptotic analysis, as well as experiments with several polymeric liquids.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas King, Eugene Pashkovski, Reid Patterson, Gareth H. McKinley

item.title: Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions for the Spectral Difference method on simplex elements
item.description: arXiv:2611.10839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unsteady compressible simulations with high-order methods on unstructured meshes require boundaries that let acoustic, entropy and vorticity waves leave the domain without spurious reflection. For the spectral difference (SD) method, the Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions (NSCBC) have only been formulated on quadrilaterals and hexahedra. Their strong-form formalism relies on a line of flux points normal to the boundary face, which does not exist on triangles and tetrahedra. This paper extends the NSCBC to the SD method on simplex elements, including multi-species reacting gases. The characteristic analysis is performed in the physical frame of each flux point of the boundary face, and the normal derivative of the normal flux is evaluated using the Raviart-Thomas divergence operator. The boundary fluxes are recovered from a linear system local to each boundary element, whose matrix depends on the geometry only. The treatment is compared with the tensor-product formulation at a comparable number of degrees of freedom on a series of test cases covering acoustic, vortical, viscous and reacting flows on triangles and tetrahedra. In all cases, the results are in close agreement with those obtained on quadrilaterals and hexahedra, so that the NSCBC become available for the SD method on simplex meshes, which are well suited to complex geometries.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Marchal, Ma\"elys Ruello, Hugues Deniau, Guillaume Daviller

item.title: Odd Darcy Law: Odd Viscosity and Edge Currents in Porous Media
item.description: arXiv:2611.11138v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We derive and numerically validate an odd Darcy law for chiral active fluids in porous media, in which an antisymmetric permeability tensor induces a flow transverse to the applied pressure gradient. We identify two distinct mechanisms leading to this odd response: odd viscosity in the fluid or the nonlinear coupling of edge currents to inertia. We then show how the transverse transport depends on porosity, boundary friction, and chirality.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Maire, Ignacio Pagonabarraga

item.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting
item.description: arXiv:2611.12193v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole's radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map's posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.
item.dc:creator: Henning Bonart

item.title: Quantitative global regularity for Navier--Stokes equations with odd viscosity on the cubic three-torus
item.description: arXiv:2611.12862v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the three-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes equation on the cubic torus with a constant odd-viscosity operator given by the vertical derivative of the curl. Arbitrary real, mean-zero, divergence-free initial data and an independent steady force, both in the second-order Sobolev space, admit a unique global strong solution when the magnitude of one fixed odd-viscosity coefficient is at least a norm-uniform sufficient threshold. In the unforced case the solution is smooth at positive times. The qualitative argument adapts the resonant-averaging framework for rapidly rotating fluids to the different odd-viscous dispersion. Weighted lattice counts and signed corrected-energy estimates yield a sufficient bound for the odd-to-ordinary viscosity ratio that is polynomial in the normalized initial-data radius at each fixed normalized force radius, together with a separate bound in a specified force-dominated regime. No optimality is claimed for the polynomial exponents or prefactors; determining the sharp viscosity threshold for the original equation remains open. Direct kinetic and weighted enstrophy barriers also give regularity for every coefficient on explicit bounded data and force regions, including the closed unforced ball of homogeneous second-order Fourier Sobolev radius ninety-seven fortieths times the viscosity and seven closed forced rectangles. We specify how finite certificates enter the analytic argument and distinguish minimization of a sufficient formula from sharpness for the original equation. All three main theorems are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
item.dc:creator: Jinzheng Li, Yuqi Li, Hao-Yu Sun

item.title: Cavitation near the oscillating piezoelectric plate in water
item.description: arXiv:1711.05234v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gas and vapor bubbles at a wall can reduce the skin friction of a liquid flow. We estimate whether an oscillating piezoelectric plate mounted flush with the wall can create such a near-wall bubble layer by acoustic cavitation. Once the cavitation threshold is reached, the liquid can no longer follow the receding plate, and the excess plate displacement is accommodated by cavitation bubbles forming at the wall; this kinematic argument gives the bubble volume generated per stroke and its energy cost. Homogeneous cavitation in pure water (about -30 MPa) requires pressure amplitudes far beyond those of flat piezoelectric plates and produces submicron bubbles that collapse within nanoseconds. Heterogeneous cavitation on wall and gas nuclei (-0.1 to -1 MPa) is within reach of piezoceramics and concentrates the void on fewer, larger wal-attached bubbles, which survive between strokes if they exceed a few micrometres at 5 MHz. The acoustic power needed to sustain a bubble layer in a turbulent boundary layer at 10 m/s is about 20 kW/m2 for heterogeneous and about 0.4 MW/m2 for homogeneous cavitation.
item.dc:creator: M. N. Shneider, M. Pekker

item.title: Design and Formulation of a Hydromechanical Fin for AUV Operations and Wave Parameter Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2306.08091v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ocean dynamics play a crucial role in global climate, ecosystems, and human activities, necessitating accurate and efficient methods to characterize ocean currents and waves. This paper presents the development of a novel bio-inspired hydrofoil system for detecting and characterizing ocean currents and waves based on a dolphin's flipper foil design. The prototype's performance was assessed through controlled experiments, demonstrating the system's ability to quickly and accurately orientate itself in the direction of flow. Wave mechanics and a geometric proof were applied to estimate wave parameters such as wave height and current from the hydrofoil's positioning. The proposed hydrofoil system shows potential for use in various marine applications, including oceanographic research, environmental monitoring, and navigation. The bio-inspired hydrofoil system offers a promising approach to ocean current and wave characterization, with the potential to significantly impact our understanding and monitoring of ocean dynamics without greatly impacting vehicle performance or increasing power utilization in operation.
item.dc:creator: Brendan M. Unikewicz

item.title: Galerkin reduced order model for two-dimensional Rayleigh-B\'enard convection
item.description: arXiv:2504.02961v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, Galerkin projection is used to build reduced-order models (ROM) for two-dimensional Rayleigh-B\'enard (RB) convection with no-slip walls. We compare an uncoupled projection approach that uses separate orthonormal bases for velocity and temperature with a coupled formalism where the equations are projected onto a single basis combining velocity and temperature components. Orthonormal bases for modal projection are obtained as the eigenfunctions of the controllability Gramian of the linearized RB equations, eliminating the need for DNS snapshot databases required by traditional POD-based approaches. Various coupled and uncoupled ROMs with different numbers of modes are generated and validated against direct numerical simulations (DNS) over a wide range of Rayleigh numbers. One of the objectives is to determine their domain of validity as a function of the system dimension and the Rayleigh number. DNS and ROM results are compared in terms of mean vertical profiles, heat flux, flow structures, dynamical regimes and energy spectra. Crucially, unlike previous POD-based Galerkin models for thermal convection, these ROMs do not require closure models and remain numerically stable. The coupled approach shows better agreement with DNS in terms of mean vertical profiles and Nusselt number scaling. The capabilities of these models are exploited to conduct a detailed bifurcation analysis at $Pr = 10$ using Poincar\'e sections and Lyapunov exponents, precisely identifying the transitions between periodic, quasiperiodic, and chaotic states with significant reductions of computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Enrique Flores-Montoya, Andr\'e V. G. Cavalieri

item.title: Significant heat transfer enhancement via polymer additives in two-dimensional sheared convection
item.description: arXiv:2605.06657v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Heat dissipation is critical in modern engineering and polymer additives offer a potential route to improve fluid-based cooling. We study elasticity-enhanced heat transfer in two-dimensional, thermally stratified Poiseuille flow. At Reynolds numbers $Re \lesssim 1000$, we observe two linearly unstable modes: the recently identified elasticity-induced centre mode (Khalid \textit{et al.}, \textit{J. Fluid Mech.}\@\ \textbf{915}, 2021) and the classical buoyancy-driven convective mode (Kelly, \textit{Adv. Appl. Mech.}\@\nobreakspace\textbf{31}, 35--112, 1994). Direct numerical simulations show that the centre mode develops into a nonlinear `arrowhead' state but yields negligible heat transfer enhancement (typically $\approx 0.03\%$ above the conductive state). By contrast, polymers can enhance the heat flux associated with the convective mode by up to $1100\%$. The nonlinear convective-mode states are periodic orbits or travelling waves, dominated by hook-like polymer-stress structures that can attach to channel walls. Both unattached and attached hooks act as `polymer walls', steering flow along rather than across them. Unattached hooks deflect fluid vertically around them in the channel interior and reduce flow rate, whereas wall-attached hooks travel more slowly, reorganising the flow into strong counter-rotating rolls and triggering extreme enhancement. The elasto-buoyant nature of these states is confirmed by perturbation kinetic energy budgets, showing that polymer and buoyancy sustain the states synergistically. Wall-attached hooks enable rapid thermal equilibration but impose a large hydraulic penalty, making them suitable for process streams requiring fast temperature adjustment. Unattached hooks provide a more thermally efficient regime for heat transport. These results highlight the potential of elastic fluids for future heat transfer enhancement technologies.
item.dc:creator: Guanhan Li, Lu Zhu, Rich. R. Kerswell

item.title: Quasi-DNS with chemical kinetics for a single multiple-injection burner element under stable lean conditions for future gas turbine applications
item.description: arXiv:2605.24226v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a Quasi-DNS with chemical kinetics for a stable lean condition in a single multiple-injection burner element for future gas turbine applications, as a reusable workflow for a coaxial mixing-tube burner. Here, Quasi-DNS denotes a high-resolution, turbulence-model-free calculation; it is not DNS in the strict sense. The OpenFOAM-based method includes: (i) a simplified 30deg sector geometry capturing vortices at the mixing tube outlet, (ii) boundary conditions reproducing coaxial jets and preheated air, (iii) a reduced Correa methane-air mechanism compared with GRI 3.0 using Cantera, (iv) mesh-development and grid-sensitivity assessment based on flame structure and the squared gradient of mixture fraction, and (v) post-processing with methane-based flame index. Demonstration at an equivalence ratio phi = 0.45 shows limited in-tube mixing and strong outlet vortices, yielding a more extended heat release region than the RANS solution. - A reusable high-resolution, turbulence-model-free Quasi-DNS workflow with detailed methane-air chemistry is developed for a coaxial mixing-tube burner. - The workflow combines a reduced methane-air mechanism, refined sector-domain meshes, and scalar-field diagnostics for characterizing mixing and heat release regions. - The workflow enables analysis of mixing and flame stabilization under stable lean conditions, and provides a high-resolution numerical reference under the stated assumptions for comparison with RANS-based calculations.
item.dc:creator: Kazuki Abe, Youhi Morii, Kaoru Maruta

item.title: Deep Learning-based Algebraic Reynolds Stress Closures for RANS Simulations of Turbulent Flows
item.description: arXiv:2605.26358v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Turbulence is ubiquitous in engineering and science, yet direct simulation is prohibitively expensive. The Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations provide savings exceeding ten orders of magnitude but introduce unclosed terms. Offline-trained machine-learning (ML) closures suffer distribution shift in predictive simulations, while ML methods that bypass the governing equations struggle to generalise from scarce high-fidelity data. We develop a physics-derived deep learning closure for RANS, the Deep Algebraic Reynolds Stress Model (DARSM), which can be trained on one or two flow cases and accurately generalise across an order of magnitude in Reynolds number, to unseen geometries, and across flow regimes. A neural network maps flow invariants to empirical parameters in an implicit algebraic Reynolds stress equation, derived from the Reynolds stress transport equations under the weak-equilibrium assumption, imposing physics-based structure on the ML closure. End-to-end optimisation through the governing PDEs eliminates distribution shift, but both unrolled and implicit automatic differentiation fail on the stiff coupled solver. We derive adjoint equations that exploit the solver's implicit-explicit structure for efficient optimisation. On canonical square-duct and periodic-hill benchmarks, DARSM reduces average test velocity error over baseline RANS by 2-4x across Reynolds number, geometries, and flow regimes, with peak case-level reductions of 12x. The model trained on attached, anisotropy-dominated flows (square duct) accurately generalises without retraining to separated flows (periodic hills), a regime change in the underlying physics. DARSM also outperforms established ML methods: offline training, tensor-basis neural networks, field-inversion machine learning, DeepONets, physics-informed neural networks, and an adjoint-trained source-term closure.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Dehtyriov, Jonathan F. MacArt, Justin Sirignano

item.title: State estimation of Rayleigh-B\'enard convection with reduced-order models
item.description: arXiv:2606.20511v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we develop a state estimation framework for two-dimensional Rayleigh-B\'enard (RB) convection that combines a stable Galerkin reduced-order model (ROM) with an extended Kalman filter (EKF). The ROM, constructed from controllability modes of the linearized Boussinesq equations, provides the nonlinear dynamical model for the filter prediction step. Direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to generate synthetic measurements for data assimilation. We assess filter performance across periodic, quasiperiodic, and chaotic regimes, demonstrating that the filter tracks the most energetic modes with high fidelity and achieves time-averaged reconstruction errors below $16\%$ for velocity and $19\%$ for temperature. We apply the ROM-based EKF to a hybrid simulation scenario where the system state is assimilated from velocity measurements. It is shown that velocity observations alone suffice to reconstruct the state, including the temperature field. Finally, we exploit the Kalman gain matrix to develop a greedy sensor placement strategy that progressively removes the least informative sensors. The algorithm reveals a clear hierarchy among sensor types and can be used to derive skeletal observation configurations. It also provides guidance on which measurement variables and spatial locations are most informative for state correction. The present framework is general, and may be applied to other quadratic Galerkin ROMs for state estimation.
item.dc:creator: Enrique Flores-Montoya, Andr\'e F. C. da Silva, Andr\'e V. G. Cavalieri

item.title: Dynamics of fluid-fluid displacements in a model rough fracture beyond the quasistatic limit: A spectral approach
item.description: arXiv:2607.23759v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In fluid-fluid displacements in porous and fractured materials, viscous friction in microscale interfacial (Haines) jumps is intimately linked to macroscale energy dissipation and the associated pressure-saturation (retention) hysteresis. The mode of control (flow rate vs. pressure) and the driving rate (from quasistatic to finite) can substantially affect hysteresis. Despite the significance of hysteresis and dissipation in various technological and natural processes, a quantitative understanding of the link between the micro- and macro-scales, and of the impact of the inherent heterogeneity of porous media, remains elusive. An ``imperfect'' Hele-Shaw cell of variable aperture is a simple model system which allows to study all these in details. However, simulating fluid-fluid interface evolution in heterogeneous media, even in such a simple system, is computationally prohibitive, as multiple length and time scales need to be resolved simultaneously. We develop here a spectral computational approach for interface evolution and energy dissipation and validate it via comparison to computational fluid dynamics simulations and experiments. Computational efficiency is demonstrated by following interface evolution in a cell with a single ``defect'', as well as with random roughness; in both, disparate length scales lead to nontrivial dynamics over many orders of magnitude in time. We also show theoretically that, in the quasi-static limit, while viscous forces during Haines jumps fully account for the energy dissipated between consecutive metastable equilibria, viscosity does not change the total dissipated amount, merely the relaxation time. Our approach provides a stepping stone towards upscaling of fluid-fluid flows in porous media.
item.dc:creator: Mykyta Chubynsky, Jordi Ortin, Marco Dentz, Ran Holtzman

item.title: How the elastic axis folds the transonic flutter boundary: shock energy transfer and conformally calibrated active learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.23298v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Isogai's case A, a pitch-plunge aerofoil whose elastic axis lies half a chord ahead of the leading edge, has a folded transonic flutter boundary in inviscid flow, with several flutter speeds at one Mach number. We map this boundary and its elastic-axis family with coupled Euler simulations, a Gaussian-process surrogate of the damping trained by batch active learning, and distribution-free split conformal prediction, which bounds the marginal error rate of stability calls. Three failure modes of damping labels are invisible in the residuals, and the half-degree mean incidence left by an impulsive start at $1^\circ$ freestream incidence raises the flutter speed at the dip by 2.8%, more than any numerical setting. With 80 simulations the learned case A boundary labels 63 of 64 independent runs correctly, and at most 1.8% of calibrated calls on held-out runs are wrong. Over Mach number, elastic axis and flutter speed index, 193 simulations show that, for the case A structure about the axis, the inviscid fold exists only for axes more than about 0.4 chord ahead of the leading edge, on two meshes. Chordwise energy budgets, closed three ways, explain both branches. On the lower branch the falling reduced frequency, at unchanged shock phase, raises the shock input and lowers the upstream damping similarly. On the upper branch the shock is pinned at the trailing edge; moving the axis aft brings the flutter-mode pivot towards the section, so the upstream damping falls faster than the residual shock input and the fold closes.
item.dc:creator: Ashray Saxena, Sharad Shrivastava

item.title: Convection in the interior of Cepheid variable stars
item.description: arXiv:2611.07142v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper is associated with a poster winner of a 2025 American Physical Society's Division of Fluid Dynamics (DFD) Gallery of Fluid Motion Award for work presented at the DFD Gallery of Fluid Motion. The original poster is available online at the Gallery of Fluid Motion, https://doi.org/10.1103/APS.DFD.2025.GFM.P005.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Stuck, Jane Pratt

item.title: Low-Rank Tensor Manifolds for Turbulent Field Reconstruction from Sparse Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.08411v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reconstructing turbulent flow fields from sparse and irregular measurements remains challenging because the underlying inverse problem is severely underdetermined. Here we present MANTRA, a manifold-based tensor framework that represents each velocity component in a continuous tensor-product space while constraining its coefficient tensor to a low-rank Tucker manifold. This structure provides a compact, data-adaptive representation without requiring gridded observations or governing equations. Riemannian optimization and adaptive selection of rank and basis complexity enable the model to exploit coordinate-wise spatiotemporal correlations. In simulations of forced isotropic turbulence and flow over a cylinder, MANTRA recovers multiscale structures at sampling densities orders of magnitude below the underlying grids and remains accurate under Gaussian noise up to 20% of the peak velocity. It also recovers leading coordinate-wise correlation structures from sparse observations. Applied to experimental particle-tracking velocimetry of an oscillating impinging jet, MANTRA reveals time-evolving structures that are not apparent from the scattered measurements alone.
item.dc:creator: Nazmus Sakib, Alexander G. Mychkovsky, Hessam Babaee

item.title: GLOBE: Accurate Surrogates for Boundary-Driven PDEs via Domain-Inspired Architectures and Equivariance
item.description: arXiv:2511.15856v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce GLOBE, a nonlinear neural surrogate for boundary-driven, homogeneous, weakly nonlinear PDEs that draws inductive bias from boundary-element methods and equivariant ML, representing solutions as superpositions of learnable Green's-function-like kernels evaluated from boundary faces to targets. The architecture is translation-, rotation-, and parity-equivariant; discretization-invariant; and units-invariant via rigorous nondimensionalization. On AirFRANS (steady incompressible RANS over NACA airfoils), a compact ~117k-parameter GLOBE model has lower mean-squared error than published values for the strongest reported ML surrogates on both the interpolation and low-data splits, in single-run comparisons under the released AirFRANS normalization. The model evaluates fields at arbitrary points, handles non-watertight meshes, and generalizes under Reynolds number and angle-of-attack distribution shifts. We further introduce a hierarchical Barnes-Hut acceleration that exploits the kernel's far-field decay to reduce evaluation cost from quadratic to near-linear in the number of boundary elements, with a tunable opening angle that recovers exact dense evaluation in the zero-angle limit. Quantitative validation focuses on 2D AirFRANS; on 3D DrivAerML cars, GLOBE predicts surface and volume fields on the full meshes, and we compare it with a matched Transolver baseline. Together, these results show that boundary-element-inspired inductive biases can substantially improve the accuracy of ML surrogates for boundary-driven PDEs while scaling to large 3D meshes.
item.dc:creator: Peter Sharpe

item.title: Linear Generator Networks for Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
item.description: arXiv:2603.29264v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most physical systems are governed by nonlinear partial differential equations, yet the analytical tools that make linear systems transparent, such as eigenspectra, dispersion relations and modal decomposition, remain unavailable in nonlinear settings. We introduce Linear Generator Network-Koopman (LGN-KM), a neural operator that learns a nonlinear lift and a continuous-time linear generator for the lifted dynamics through the decomposition $L_k = S - D_k$, where $S$ is skew-symmetric (conservative coupling) and $D_k$ is positive-definite diagonal (mode-selective dissipation). The decomposition guarantees stability by construction and exposes the eigenstructure directly, making linear-systems analysis available on a nonlinear PDE. On 2D Navier-Stokes turbulence, the generator yields a complete multi-branch dispersion relation and models trained independently at viscosities $100\times$ apart learn the same coupling spectrum ($R^2 = 0.87$). The same architecture shows the corresponding diffusive damping on FitzHugh-Nagumo reaction-diffusion, and for pulse propagation in optical fibers, the oscillation frequencies of the learned generator match the fiber's dispersion relation, giving the group-velocity dispersion to within $3.1\%$ with no fitted constant. The architecture additionally enables long-horizon stability, $O(1)$ continuous-time evaluation, and physics-informed cross-regime model transfer.
item.dc:creator: Shafayeth Jamil, Rehan Kapadia

item.title: The $L^p$ spectrum of the Stokes operator on hyperbolic 3-space and exponential decay for the Navier-Stokes equations
item.description: arXiv:2605.22212v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We determine the $L^p$ spectrum, $1<p<\infty$, of the Stokes operator $A=-\PP\LD$ on divergence-free vector fields of hyperbolic 3-space of curvature $-a^2$, where $\LD=\Delta_B+\Ric$ is the Ebin-Marsden deformation Laplacian and $\PP$ is the Leray projector. The spectrum is the parabolic region $a^2\{4+z^2:\ z\in\C,\ |\im z|\le|1-2/p|\}$. For $p>2$ every interior point is an eigenvalue, realized by an explicit family of divergence-free swirl fields which leave $L^p$ exactly at the boundary of the region. It follows that the Stokes semigroup on $\Lp$ has exponential type exactly $-\mu_p$ with $\mu_p=a^2\bigl(4-(1-2/p)^2\bigr)$. At $p=3$ this is $35a^2/9$, which lies strictly above the rates $26a^2/9$ and $10a^2/3$ that follow from pointwise domination by the scalar heat semigroup and from interpolation, and strictly below the $L^2$ gap $4a^2$. For the Navier-Stokes equations with small data in $L^3$, whose global solvability on $\HH^3$ is due to Pierfelice, the solutions decay in $L^3$ and in $L^6$ at every rate below $\mu\cdot35a^2/9$, where $\mu$ is the viscosity, and no faster rate holds for the linearized flow. The exponent $3$ is the usual scaling threshold. Curvature fixes the time scale of the decay and introduces no new threshold.
item.dc:creator: Zhi-Wei Wang, Samuel L. Braunstein

item.title: Self-similar structure of non-isothermal variable-density mushy Stefan problems and an improved low-Mach enthalpy method
item.description: arXiv:2608.00960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The enthalpy method was introduced in the late 1970s to simulate phase-change problems on fixed grids without explicitly tracking the moving phase-change front. It remains one of the most widely used approaches in academic and commercial software for the simulation of industrial melting and solidification processes. For pure phase-change materials (PCMs) that melt or solidify at a single temperature, the enthalpy method introduces an artificial mushy region bounded by the solidus temperature, $T^{\rm sol}$, and the liquidus temperature, $T^{\rm liq}$. As the numerical parameter $\Delta T=T^{\rm liq}- T^{\rm sol}$ approaches zero, the solution obtained with the enthalpy method is generally assumed to converge to that of the classical Stefan problem, in which the phase-change front is infinitesimally thin. This assumption is largely based on benchmark studies performed under the simplifying assumption of equal solid and liquid densities. In this work, we systematically investigate the accuracy and spatio-temporal convergence properties of the enthalpy method for both low- and high-density-ratio phase-change problems. Because the limiting behavior $\Delta T\rightarrow0$ is difficult to realize numerically, owing to the diminishing thickness of the mushy region, we formulate and analyze the finite-$\Delta T$ mushy Stefan problem solved by the enthalpy method. We show that this problem possesses a self-similar structure that reduces the governing equations to a boundary-value problem involving two unknown parameters. The theoretical analysis also enables improvements to our previously developed low-Mach enthalpy method, enhancing its stability and accuracy as the density ratio between the two phases increases from $\mathcal{O}(1)$ to $\mathcal{O}(3)$.
item.dc:creator: Yavkreet Swami, Amneet Pal Singh Bhalla

item.title: Evaluation of the Ambipolar Diffusion Approximation in Partially Ionized Rarefied Hypersonic Flows
item.description: arXiv:2608.12498v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate numerical simulation of rarefied hypersonic plasmas is increasingly important for optimization of re-entry spacecraft design and the development of advanced aerospace technologies. For kinetic simulation methods, it is convention to enforce ions and electrons to diffuse at the same rate, known as the ambipolar diffusion approximation. This approach circumvents costly resolution of fast electron motion, but neglects the complex plasma dynamics of ions and electrons. Almost all studies that investigated the efficacy of the ambipolar diffusion approximation in hypersonics report noticeable differences in flowfield properties when electrostatic modeling is used, including increases in vehicle surface heat flux and decreases in electron temperature. However, studying the ambipolar diffusion approximation in multi-species hypersonic flows (such as air flows) makes it challenging to isolate the origin of these differences. Kinetic hypersonic flow simulations with electrostatic modeling are performed with argon to quantify the validity of the ambipolar diffusion approximation along a one-dimensional stagnation streamline. Three different plasma diffusion regimes are studied under two sets of rarefied freestream flow conditions. The approximation is evaluated in terms of predicting plasma density distributions, electron temperature, and stagnation point heat flux. New criteria are proposed for identification of plasma diffusion regimes in hypersonic flows and use of the ambipolar diffusion approximation.
item.dc:creator: Marisa Petrusky, Iain D. Boyd

item.title: Universal Scaling and Geometric Correction of High-Frequency Mass Transfer in Porous Electrodes
item.description: arXiv:2610.20211v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Classical film theory predicts a finite diffusion-limited current at porous electrodes. Transient operation can nevertheless produce peak interfacial fluxes above this steady limit, although the time-averaged flux remains bounded. Here, we use a frequency-domain volume-averaging framework to study this transient response in porous media. In the perfectly reactive limit, the spectral Sherwood number approaches $\Shnd\sim\sqrt{\iu\wstar}$ at high frequency, with magnitude proportional to $\omega^{1/2}$, phase $\pi/4$, and a universal leading prefactor. A boundary-layer analysis shows that this response follows from local transient diffusion and is independent of the global pore geometry. Numerical results for parallel plates, circular tubes, and twelve porous microstructures confirm the scaling across variations in particle shape, symmetry, porosity, array arrangement, flow orientation, and flow strength. We also derive the first geometry-dependent correction, which depends on interfacial area, surface curvature, and sharp edges, and verify it without fitted parameters. Comparisons with published impedance measurements for a carbon-felt fiber and a vanadium flow-battery electrode are consistent with the predicted transport response. Finally, we derive bounds on pulse duration and identify operating windows for representative redox couples. These results establish a temporal route to enhanced peak transport in porous electrodes without requiring surface charge, confinement, or electrokinetic instability.
item.dc:creator: Md Abdul Hamid, Kyle C. Smith
